disclaimer: This report is for educational and wellness purposes only. It is not a medical diagnosis and does not replace advice from a qualified healthcare professional. HbA1c results should be confirmed by your doctor. Do not start, stop or change any medication without medical advice.

status.label: In the diabetes range
status.explanation: Your HbA1c is 6.5% or above, the range used to diagnose diabetes. A single result is not a diagnosis: your doctor will confirm it with a repeat test or another blood test.

summary: Your HbA1c is in the diabetes range, which means your body is having more trouble managing blood sugar than is ideal. This is happening alongside several other factors, including obesity, low activity, smoking, and existing conditions like high blood pressure, high cholesterol, kidney and liver concerns, and sleep apnoea, all of which can interact with blood sugar control. The most valuable next steps are getting your lipid profile, kidney function, and liver checks done soon, building in regular gentle movement, and following the eating pattern outlined in your plan. These changes, done consistently, can meaningfully improve how you feel and lower your risks over time.

risk_factors.label: Existing health condition: High blood pressure
Existing health condition: High cholesterol or triglycerides
Existing health condition: Heart or blood-vessel disease
Existing health condition: Fatty liver disease

comorbidity_assessment.note: High blood pressure often travels with elevated blood sugar and adds strain to your heart and blood vessels, so keeping both in check together is important.
Unhealthy cholesterol levels can build on the vascular stress caused by higher blood sugar, raising the importance of heart-healthy eating and activity.
Carrying extra body weight makes it harder for your body to use insulin effectively, so gradual weight loss can directly help blood sugar control.
Blood sugar in the diabetes range can add extra pressure on your heart and blood vessels, making regular cardiovascular monitoring especially valuable.
Elevated blood sugar can affect kidney function over time, so tracking kidney markers closely is important for your overall health.
Thyroid imbalances can affect energy, weight, and sometimes blood sugar levels, so keeping thyroid function monitored helps you understand your overall picture.
Extra fat in the liver is closely linked with insulin resistance, meaning liver health and blood sugar often improve together with weight loss.
Poor sleep quality from sleep apnoea can make blood sugar harder to manage, so treating it consistently may support better glucose control.

constraints: Keep sodium under 2,300 mg a day (about one teaspoon of salt in total); avoid pickles, papad, instant noodles and salty snacks.
Follow a DASH-style pattern rich in vegetables, fruit, pulses and low-fat dairy (or fortified alternatives).
Keep saturated fat low (limit ghee, butter, coconut oil, red and processed meat); avoid trans fats (vanaspati, many fried and bakery foods).
Include soluble fibre daily (oats, barley, pulses, psyllium) and unsaturated fats (nuts, seeds, olive or mustard oil in small amounts).
Follow the calorie target; avoid sugary drinks and fruit juices completely.
Fill half the plate with non-starchy vegetables to stay full on fewer calories.
Keep sodium under 2,300 mg a day and saturated fat low.
Prefer fish, pulses and nuts over red and processed meat (plant proteins for vegetarian and vegan users).
Do not follow high-protein diets or take protein supplements; keep protein moderate unless your kidney doctor advises otherwise.
Do not use potassium-based salt substitutes; ask your doctor whether you need to limit potassium or phosphorus.
Do not take iodine or kelp supplements unless prescribed.
Cut added sugars and sugary drinks, especially fructose-sweetened ones.
Avoid alcohol and heavy meals within 3 hours of bedtime.

foods_to_eat: Non-starchy vegetables like spinach, bottle gourd, bhindi, broccoli and carrots
Whole grains and millets such as oats, barley, jowar and bajra
Pulses like moong dal, masoor dal and rajma
Fish such as pomfret or rohu prepared with minimal oil
Nuts and seeds like almonds, walnuts and flaxseed in small amounts
Low-fat dairy such as buttermilk and low-fat paneer
Fresh low-glycaemic fruits like guava, papaya and apple
Herbs and spices like cumin, coriander, turmeric and garlic for flavour instead of salt
foods_to_avoid: Pickles, papad and other salted preserved foods
Instant noodles and packaged salty snacks
Red and processed meat such as sausages and salami
Ghee, butter, coconut oil and vanaspati in large amounts
Deep-fried foods and bakery items made with refined flour and trans fats
Sugary drinks, fruit juices and sweetened beverages
plan.portion_guidance: Fill half your plate with non-starchy vegetables, a quarter with whole grains or millets, and a quarter with a moderate protein source like dal, fish or paneer. Use not more than 3-4 teaspoons of oil across the whole day, preferring mustard or olive oil. Keep dinner light and finish eating at least three hours before bedtime to support better sleep and digestion.
plan.hydration: Drink about 8 to 10 glasses of plain water through the day. Buttermilk and herbal teas like cumin or fennel water can count toward fluids, but avoid sugary drinks and fruit juices completely. If you have kidney concerns, check with your doctor about your ideal daily fluid amount.
based_on: HbA1c in the diabetes range: low-glycaemic, high-fibre focus
high blood pressure: DASH-style, sodium under 2,300 mg
high cholesterol: low saturated fat, unsaturated fats emphasised
obesity and sedentary activity: portion-controlled, vegetable-forward plate
kidney disease: moderate protein, no potassium salt substitutes
heart disease: reduced sodium and saturated fat
fatty liver disease: no added sugar, no alcohol
sleep apnoea: lighter evening meals, no late heavy eating
current smoker and occasional alcohol: alcohol avoided completely

exercise: Because you have heart or blood-vessel disease, please get medical clearance from your doctor before starting any new or vigorous exercise programme.
Start gently with short sessions of gentle walking or seated exercises, 5-10 minutes at a time, and build up slowly as your body allows.
Aim gradually toward 150 minutes a week of moderate activity, spread across most days, adjusting the pace based on your energy levels since thyroid problems can affect this.
Add simple muscle-strengthening movements (like sit-to-stand or light resistance bands) on 2 non-consecutive days a week, once cleared by your doctor.
Stop exercising immediately and seek help if you feel chest pain, unusual breathlessness or dizziness.
Avoid high-impact activities to protect your joints given your weight; choose low-impact options like walking in water or on flat ground.
lifestyle.walking_goal: Start with 10 minutes of gentle walking a day, 3 days a week, and build up gradually to 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week, as your fitness and energy improve.
lifestyle.weight_management: Your BMI is in the obese range, so a gradual weight loss of 5-10% of your current body weight over about 6 months is a realistic and healthy goal. This amount of weight loss can also help improve liver fat and may reduce the severity of sleep apnoea. Focus on steady, sustainable changes rather than quick fixes, and work closely with your healthcare team given your other health conditions.
lifestyle.sleep: Aim for 7-9 hours of sleep each night. Keep a regular sleep and wake schedule, even on weekends. Use your prescribed breathing device every night without fail, since this is especially important with sleep apnoea. Avoid screens and heavy meals close to bedtime, and keep your bedroom cool and dark.
stress: Try slow breathing exercises for 5-10 minutes a day, such as inhaling for a count of 4 and exhaling for a count of 6, to help calm your body.
Practice mindfulness or a short body-scan meditation daily using a free app or guided audio.
Gentle yoga or stretching can help ease tension, but check with your doctor first given your heart condition.
Spend time on hobbies or activities with family and friends to help lower everyday stress.
behaviour_change: Since you currently smoke, consider reaching out to a quitline or your doctor for support and practical strategies to stop smoking; quitting will help your heart, lungs, and overall health.
Although your alcohol use is occasional, try to keep intake low and avoid increasing it over time.
Avoid regular use of painkillers such as ibuprofen without speaking to your doctor first, as these can affect your kidneys.
Set small, specific weekly goals (like a short walk or one new vegetable dish) to build healthy habits step by step.
Keep regular follow-ups with your healthcare team to monitor your blood pressure, cholesterol, kidney function, thyroid, and liver health.

monitoring.name: Lipid profile (cholesterol)
monitoring.why: Diabetes and high cholesterol together raise the risk of heart disease and stroke.
monitoring.frequency: Every year (at least every 5 years if you are under 40), or as your doctor advises
risk_indicators: Existing cholesterol problem or heart disease

monitoring.name: Kidney function (eGFR) and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
monitoring.why: High glucose and blood pressure can quietly damage the kidneys; these tests find it early.
monitoring.frequency: Every year, or more often if you already have kidney disease

monitoring.name: Liver check (liver tests and FIB-4 score)
monitoring.why: Fatty liver is common with diabetes and obesity and can progress without symptoms.
monitoring.frequency: FIB-4 score every 1–2 years, or sooner if your doctor finds a higher risk

monitoring.name: Dilated eye examination
monitoring.why: Diabetes can damage the retina (diabetic retinopathy) long before your vision changes.
monitoring.frequency: Soon after diabetes is confirmed, then every year (your eye doctor may extend this to every 2 years if exams stay clear)

monitoring.name: Foot examination
monitoring.why: Diabetes can reduce feeling and blood flow in the feet, so small injuries go unnoticed.
monitoring.frequency: A full exam every year; check your own feet daily

monitoring.name: Blood pressure
monitoring.why: High blood pressure multiplies the heart and kidney risks of high blood glucose.
monitoring.frequency: At every doctor visit; at home regularly if you have high blood pressure

monitoring.name: Cardiovascular risk assessment
monitoring.why: Heart disease is the leading cause of death in people with diabetes.

monitoring.name: HbA1c
monitoring.why: Shows your average blood glucose over about 3 months and whether your plan is working.
monitoring.frequency: Every 3 months until your doctor says you are at target, then every 6 months

monitoring.name: Fasting blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows your blood glucose after an overnight fast and complements HbA1c.
monitoring.frequency: Alongside your HbA1c test, or as your doctor advises

monitoring.name: Post-meal (post-prandial) blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows how your body handles glucose after meals, which HbA1c alone can hide.

monitoring.name: Vitamin B12
monitoring.why: Metformin, a common diabetes medicine, can lower B12 over time; low B12 can mimic nerve damage.
monitoring.frequency: Ask your doctor, especially if you take metformin (often checked yearly)
risk_indicators: Vegetarian or vegan diet (lower dietary B12)

monitoring.name: Vitamin D
monitoring.why: Low vitamin D is more common with obesity and kidney disease; testing is not routine for everyone.
monitoring.frequency: Only if your doctor recommends it

monitoring.name: Thyroid function (TSH)
monitoring.why: Thyroid problems affect weight, energy and blood glucose control.
monitoring.frequency: Every 6–12 months, or as your doctor advises

preventive_actions: Book your lipid profile, kidney function, and liver checks as soon as you can since these are flagged as high priority.
Add short, gentle walks most days of the week and build up slowly, as cleared by your doctor.
Follow the sodium, saturated fat, and sugar limits in your food plan to support both blood sugar and heart health.
Work toward a gradual weight loss goal of 5-10% of your body weight over the next six months.
Keep a consistent sleep schedule and use any prescribed breathing support every night for your sleep apnoea.
If you smoke, consider talking to your doctor about support options for quitting, as this affects many of your risk factors.

hba1c_caveat: HbA1c can be less accurate if you have anaemia, kidney disease, a recent blood transfusion or certain haemoglobin variants.
